#6373. The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W Power Bank Is a Travel-Ready Charging Beast

This laptop charger has everything you could want in a travel power backup solution and only costs $120.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

ReelCharge, a relative newcomer to the portable battery pack market, has caught our eye this year with a few interesting options. Most notable among them is the ReelPro 200W, a compact but massively powerful laptop charger that can keep up with your travel charging needs better than any pack we’ve tested. It features an ample 27,000 milliampere-hour (mAh) battery capacity—about as much as you can get while staying under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour limit—and a maximum power output of 200 watts (W), including up to 140-watt charging on a single device. That beats most laptop wall chargers on speed. Best of all, it costs only $120, substantially undercutting flagship battery packs from legacy brands such as Anker and EcoFlow.

Throw in some premium features and a three-year warranty, and you have a power bank that truly feels like it's setting a new gold standard for high-end power banks that the competition will need to meet.

The ReelPro 200W looks like a bougie battery pack. It has a sleek housing with a matte finish, a glossy front panel, and a color LED display. A display is definitely a must for a high-capacity battery pack in the mid-2020s. It shows the battery’s remaining charge and the wattage going into each outlet, plus status checks on temperature and health. It’s neatly integrated into the pack’s glossy front panel, so it fades into it when turned off, giving it a pleasantly minimalist look.

The ReelPro can charge up to three devices—more than a little, but not the most we’ve seen. It has an integrated, retractable USB-C cable, which can loop around to become a wrist strap. There are also USB-C and USB-A ports for when you want to charge up multiple devices (and to charge the pack itself). Personally, I prefer a battery pack with an external cable to one with a retractable cord because this leaves more interior space for battery cells and allows for a larger capacity.

Having plenty of ports means little if the pack can’t power them properly, and that’s where the ReelPro 200 watts really impresses. As the name suggests, it has a total power output of 200W and can charge a single device at up to 140 watts. That’s as much as we’ve ever seen in a battery pack, and more than you’ll get out of premium wall chargers for laptops and other devices. Case in point: the official charger for the 16-inch MacBook Pro delivers the same amount of power.

Having that extra 60 watts of output means that when you plug in multiple devices, you’re less likely to see a slowdown in charging. I was able to charge my MacBook Pro and an iPhone 18 Pro Max at the same time at full speed. If you were to plug in three large devices (like laptops) at the same time, there would be a substantial drop-off in power going to the first device, but it can handle most common travel setups without that happening.

The result is a backup power solution that works just as well as plugging your devices into the wall, even when you need to charge multiple devices. On a recent weekend trip, I used it to charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro faster than its included 70-watt adapter, without exceeding 140 watts. It’s the kind of performance we all wish we could get from a battery pack, but never actually do.

This is a secondary concern, but I think it’s worth pointing out that ReelCharge offers a best-in-class three-year warranty on the ReelPro 200W. That’s a lot of protection for any piece of tech, and far longer than most competitors: Anker, for example, backs battery packs with an 18-month warranty, which is better than average. Standing by its products for so long shows the brand has strong faith in them.

If you are a frequent traveler, or a mobile worker who lives and dies by having constant access to a laptop, this is the best high-capacity battery pack I’ve tested to date. It’s definitely too big to fit in your pocket, so it’s overkill if you just need to top up a phone or tablet occasionally, but this is the ReelPro 200W, a big battery backup that you can depend on, and it costs far less than the Anker Prime, our previous laptop charger of choice.

#6372. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6371. I’m a Tape Measure Guy. But This Laser Measuring Tool is Testing My Loyalty.

Measuring long walls, gauging ceiling heights, and handling the awkward math are where the Mileseey S50C shines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Look, I’m a tape measure guy. Always have been. Always will be. That red Milwaukee 25-footer rides on my hip like Wyatt Earp’s six-shooter, ready to draw when I need fast dimensions across a 2x4 or sheet of plywood. I ask a lot of it, and it always delivers. That is, until I ask it to stretch across a long wall and maintain its rigidity.

But I got my hands on Mileseey’s S50C Laser Measure and it has me reconsidering how often I reach for my trusty tape—especially when my foe is notably larger than normal and physically out of my league. No one ever said I had to fight fair, so lately I find myself reaching for a more technologically advanced weapon of choice. And in that moment before I grab, I always have the same thought: Why am I working so hard?

What’s won me over about the S50C is how easily it takes over the measurements I least enjoy making with a tape. Long distances. Wall-to-wall dimensions. Floor-to-ceiling heights. The sort of thing that usually has me looking around for another person to whom I need to say “Hey, could you hold this for a second?” Aim, press the button, read the measurement. Nobody has to put down what they’re doing and walk over.

The S50C has been impressively accurate and simple to operate. It’s also handy as heck, which matters to me more than a long list of functions. A tool can have enough computing power to figure out a Mars landing, but if taking basic measurements becomes a small administrative project, I’m going straight back to the tape. With this one, I’ve found myself grabbing it as soon as a measurement starts feeling like it’s going to give me a fight, which is exactly how any new tool tends to earn a home in my usual routine.

The S50C also goes way beyond telling you how far away the opposite wall is. You can easily toggle through its measurement modes on the touch screen display to select area, volume, and wall area calculations, along with more specialized functions for awkward dimensions. For something like a basement renovation, that means you can gather room dimensions and calculate floor area without balancing a notebook on your knee or pulling up the calculator app on your phone. For painting, wall-area calculations give you a useful starting point for estimating coverage. You still have to account for multiple coats, product coverage, and waste—I mean, this device isn’t going to manage your entire renovation. But it can take a welcome chunk of arithmetic off your plate.

The trick is choosing the proper mode and taking the measurements it requests. It isn’t one magical button that automatically understands your basement. You supply the dimensions by placing the green laser dot on the opposing wall or ceiling, press the button, and record the measurement. The S50C handles the rest of the calculations.

The S50C has a built-in camera with up to 8x zoom—but it’s for helping you aim at distant targets. A 2.4-inch AMOLED touch screen displays the targeting view, measurements, and menus. That gives the camera a practical reason to exist. Finding a little laser dot at a distance—especially outdoors measuring distances for a fence installation—can become its own project and a huge source of frustration. The camera is there to help you see where you’re aiming, which is great for me and my ever-flagging eyesight.

Mileseey lists a maximum measuring range of 670 feet. I’ve yet to verify that distance without putting the laser on my neighbor’s home five houses away from me, but it does give you some semblance of the work this device is designed to accommodate. It also charges through USB-C and carries an IP65 dust- and water-resistance rating.

There are plenty of measurements for which I’ll keep pulling my tape. Most, come to think of it. Marking a board for a miter saw cut, checking a short dimension, laying something out directly on a workpiece. That familiar steel blade is like an extension of my hand most times.

But the S50C is worth grabbing when distance, access, or a shortage of available hands suddenly turns that tape measure into a nuisance. Its more advanced functions expand the possibilities, I suppose, but its quick convenience is what brings me back in those moments of need. On that note, if you think your measuring needs are more basic in nature, Mileseey’s S50 PrecisionX model is an ideal alternative to all of those extra features of the S50C.

I really didn’t expect to become attached to a laser measure, let alone one with so many bells and whistles. But then my tape buckled halfway across my ceiling, and the S50C gadget was sitting right there waiting.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6369. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

#6368. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6367. Bees make a natural plastic that starts breaking down in soil within months

Solitary bees make natural plastic that breaks down in soil, offering clues for designing less persistent synthetic materials.

A plastic wrapper may be useful for a few minutes, then stay in the environment for centuries. But a small bee makes a plastic-like material that starts breaking down in soil within months.

The bee, Colletes inaequalis, uses it to cover the inside of its underground nest. The material helps protect the young bee growing inside.

Researchers studied these nests in Tennessee. In fresh nests, plastic made up 73% of the lining’s weight, but four months later, that share had fallen to 40%.

Now the team wants to learn how the bee makes a material that is tough but still breaks down. The answer could help scientists make better plastics for everyday use.

Jonathan Coote, an assistant professor at Virginia Tech, led the study.

Laura Russo, who studies bees at the University of Tennessee, first told him about the material while he was a doctoral student there.

Coote kept studying it during his later research at the University of Minnesota. After joining Virginia Tech in 2025, he made it his main research focus.

Scientists identified the chemical makeup of the bee’s plastic more than 45 years ago. But for years afterward, few people studied it further.

Most bees live alone rather than in hives. This species, common in the eastern United States, digs tunnels in the ground and builds small rooms for its young.

The female covers each room with a thin, clear layer, which gives these insects the name cellophane bees. She adds pollen and nectar, lays one egg, and closes the room.

The young bee spends more than 90% of its life inside. The lining likely protects it and its food from water and fungus.

The lining contains silk and a natural plastic made by the female.

A gland connected to her stinger releases tiny, ring-shaped molecules, which join into long chains as she spreads them over the walls.

The bee’s material resembles polyethylene, a plastic widely used in packaging.

Polyethylene contains long chains of carbon atoms held together by strong bonds that are hard to break, even in industrial compost.

Only about 9% of the world’s plastic was recycled in 2022. Nearly a third is poorly managed and ends up in the environment, where it can break into tiny pieces called microplastics.

Scientists have tried making similar plastics with weaker links in their chains. Water or enzymes, natural substances that help chemical reactions happen, can break these links.

These materials are called polyesters, and the bee’s plastic belongs to this group. “This is a polyester that mimics polyethylene,” Coote said.

Even with weaker links, most lab-made versions barely break down.

Their chains pack closely together and keep water out, making the weaker links hard to reach.

The best-studied version lost only 18% of its weight after 280 days in industrial compost. It did not break down at all under milder conditions.

The bee’s nests offered a clue that its material was different. More than 10,000 nests can share one site, and bees may return to the same ground for decades.

Yet the old plastic linings do not seem to pile up. Something appears to break them down.

The team first tried to dissolve the bee’s plastic to study its chains. After two days in a solvent heated to 302°F (150°C), the material still held its shape and size.

This suggested that the chains were linked together like a net.

About 60% of the plastic also formed tightly packed areas called crystals, arranged like those in polyethylene.

Usually, these tightly packed areas make plastic harder to break down. So the bee’s material seemed to have the same features that cause trouble in lab-made plastics.

The researchers collected fresh nests in March 2023 in Hamblen County, eastern Tennessee.

They returned in July and October 2023 and February 2024, digging seven to 12 inches (17 to 30 centimeters) down to find them.

After four months, the linings could still bend and hold their shape. By about seven months, when the young bees had become adults, cracks had appeared.

By 11 months, the linings crumbled when handled roughly. They had not vanished, but they were falling apart.

At first, the lining was about 73% plastic and 27% silk by weight. After four months, plastic made up only 40% of the remaining lining.

Silk usually breaks down fairly quickly, so the team was surprised to find the plastic breaking down even faster.

Later, the balance changed less, suggesting both materials were then breaking down at roughly the same pace.

Tightly packed regions accounted for about 60% of the plastic initially and nearly 100% of the remaining plastic after four months. By 11 months, their share had fallen to 39%.

This suggests the looser parts broke down first. The tightly packed parts appear to have broken down later.

The answer may lie in the plastic’s tiny building blocks. Most are rings with 18 carbon atoms, while some have 20 or 22.

Mixing these sizes may spread the weaker links unevenly along the chains. That could leave more links where water and enzymes can reach them.

The tightly packed areas are also small and less orderly, which could help. Microbes in the nest may also play a part.

Another idea involves an enzyme in the bee’s saliva. It might help build the plastic, then help break it down later.

The researchers rinsed the linings three times and collected the liquid. They added a chemical that this kind of enzyme can break apart.

Liquid from both a new lining and a four-month-old lining broke down the chemical. This suggests enzymes could keep working in the nest for months.

But the test used only one new nest and one older nest. More tests are needed to find out what those enzymes actually do.

The team still does not know which explanation matters most. Each nest provides only a few milligrams of lining, so some tests ran just once or twice, and all the older nests came from one site.

“The goal is to be able to answer that and then engineer it into something that we can make at scale. I don’t see a future where we have these massive bee farms making all of our plastic products,” Coote said.

If the spacing of the weaker links is the key, scientists could try copying it. They want a useful plastic that can break down in soil after its job is done.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6366. Jackery’s FridgeGuard Brings Basic Automated Backup Power at an Affordable Price

Our tests show that during short blackouts, this automated backup power system gets the job done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not every home power backup solution has to be an expensive and complicated system. Certainly, a portable power station can be affordable, but it usually has to be set up when the power goes out, which isn’t convenient if you’re not at home. What if you could meet in the middle with something affordable but also automated? That’s the aim of a device like Jackery’s FridgeGuard, an automated appliance backup device that costs less than $800.

It’s named FridgeGuard because Jackery, like competitors Bluetti and BioLite (whose products we also reviewed), is banking on the idea that the appliance most people care about powering when the lights go out is the refrigerator. It makes sense; you’ve got the most to lose with spoiled food during an extended blackout. But in truth, you can use this type of backup with any alternating-current-powered device, whether that is a fish tank, automatic pet feeder, garage freezer, or even essential medical equipment. And since this is designed to be always-on, you don’t have to think about it very much once you set it up.

Out of the box, the Jackery FridgeGuard is smaller and lighter than the competition. It’s a few inches shorter than those from Bluetti and BioLite, and only weighs 23 pounds—the others weigh more than 40 pounds. That makes the task of placing this out of the way, either mounted on a cabinet or sitting flat on top of a cabinet, a bit easier. It also has two airflow vents that you can remove to clean or replace filters, which is a nice feature to have in a kitchen, where air particles can be heavier from cooking.

Cutting down on the size keeps the price point lower, but this comes at another cost. At 1,024 watt-hours of battery capacity, FridgeGuard can’t run a refrigerator for as long as the competition, and with only 800 watts of output (roughly half the amount or more of the others), you can’t run as many things from it. There’s also only one outlet, as opposed to two, so if you want to power more than one thing, you’ll need to attach a power strip.

Of course, this may not matter to people who really are only concerned about keeping their refrigerator running. I tested this out on my own full-size French-door, bottom-freezer model, and I was able to run it for 11 hours. That’s enough time for most people experiencing a blackout after a severe storm. If you find that’s not enough, you can always add the FridgeGuard battery pack and double that capacity to 2,048 watt-hours.

There are some other hidden cost-cutting measures, too. Jackery includes attachable feet if you want to stand it vertically, but wall mounts are optional ($29), and if you want to recharge it using a portable solar panel, you’ll need to purchase a proprietary adapter that costs $89. Competitors include wall mounts, and solar inputs are built into their units.

Despite some cost cutting with its hardware, FridgeGuard doesn’t skimp on smart features within the app. If you're away from home, you get notifications when the power goes out and when the FridgeGuard is starting to get low on power. If you live in a region with variable utility rates, you can set it to only recharge from grid power when the rates are at their lowest (your electric company can tell you when that is).

Conversely, you can also use it to save a bit of money by using a time-of-use (TOU) mode that powers the fridge from the battery during high-rate hours and grid power only during the low-rate hours. It would take many months of testing to see how much money you could really save using this mode, but the potential is there.

Some may worry about daily discharge and recharge, but FridgeGuard runs on a lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery that offers up to 6,000 recharge cycles, which is 16 years if you were to do it every day. In the end, TOU mode may be worth it.

If all you want is automated backup power for your refrigerator (or another essential appliance or device) for a few hours, Jackery’s FridgeGuard is the simplest and most economical way to go. It’s easy to set up and the epitome of instant automation. If you frequently experience blackouts longer than 12 hours, spending a bit more on a system from Bluetti or BioLite may suit your needs better, but if not, Jackery has built a good product for you.

#6365. When rain returns after a drought, groundwater reserves don’t always get caught up before the next drought

Most groundwater refills faster than it drains in a drought, but in about a quarter of places, the next drought hits before recovery ends.

When a drought breaks, the rain returns first, then the soil moisture, the plants and the rivers. Groundwater usually comes last, and in some places the next drought arrives before it has caught up.

A new global analysis suggests that, in most places, groundwater refills faster than it drains during a drought. But across about a quarter of the places studied, water levels tended to slip back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That matters because groundwater supplies roughly 35 percent of all the fresh water people withdraw, and it’s the reserve many communities rely on when rivers run low.

Hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth led the work with three colleagues at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. Their results come from a computer model rather than direct measurements.

It estimates how deep you’d have to dig to reach water, a level called the water table, month by month from 1960 to 2019.

This model divides the world’s land into squares about 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) across. It was developed at Utrecht’s Department of Physical Geography, and it tracks both the rain that soaks into soil and the water people pump out of it.

Checked against real wells, the model gave useful estimates at about 80 percent of wells shallower than about 200 feet (60 meters). For deeper wells, the figure was about 70 percent.

For every square and every calendar month, the team worked out how deep the water table usually was and how much that depth normally varied.

A drought started when the groundwater dropped so far below its usual level for that time of year that only about 16 percent of months would qualify. It ended when the water rose back above that line.

Droughts lasting two months or less were left out, because monthly data can’t capture them reliably. For the rest, the team measured how fast the water fell, how fast it rose again, and what it did in the six months afterward.

Climate did more than anything else to set the pace of recovery. Places where a lot of rain soaks into the ground, such as the Amazon and Southeast Asia, recovered quickly. Their droughts also tended to be shorter and more frequent.

Dry regions recovered slowly. The slow places included Australia, the Middle East and Central Asia, southern Africa, southern South America and the U.S. Midwest.

During drought recovery, the groundwater at a typical location rose about 0.7 inches (1.8 centimeters) a month. In the fastest places it climbed as much as about 3 feet (1 meter) a month.

Those raw speeds partly reflect how much a water table swings in an ordinary year. So the team also compared each place with its own normal range, and the split between wet and dry regions became sharper.

Average speed told only part of the story. Two places could recover at the same average rate and still behave very differently during a drought.

Hauswirth hadn’t expected recovery to vary so much within a single region. In an interview with Earth.com, she said, “I was surprised to see that the groundwater recovery pattern was not necessarily homogeneous within a region and could vary quite a bit locally.”

To capture those differences, the team sorted every location by how its droughts unfolded. About 57 percent were resilient: on average, the water came back faster than it had dropped. Another 26 percent were unstable, slipping back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That makes the unstable group the second largest. The researchers described its behavior as even more critical than that of the vulnerable group, where the water fell quickly and climbed back slowly.

The unstable group covered about 15 percent of places, and only around 2 percent were stable, with the fall and the rise at about the same speed.

Unstable places weren’t clustered in one part of the world, and they weren’t limited to heavily pumped areas. Their droughts were shorter, milder and more frequent than in any other group, often with little time to refill in between.

Terrain set the vulnerable places apart. In every region the team examined up close, they turned up at higher elevations, where the ground stores less water and the water table swings more widely.

In Europe, some may be linked to limestone country, where water drains through cracks and caves.

The close-ups included California, Spain, India and the North China Plain, all places known for heavy groundwater use. In Spain, the vulnerable and unstable spots shared similar pumping patterns. In California, pumping appeared to affect more of the categories.

Sorting places this way, Hauswirth said, made it clear that local features “are an important part of the drivers and should not be underestimated.”

For water managers in vulnerable regions, her advice starts with knowing where the water comes from. Where possible, she said, they should map how much of local demand and supply is covered by groundwater.

That “could help us better understand when groundwater resources are overexploited,” she told Earth.com, and when a wet spell could help restore levels, possibly by cutting back on pumping.

The authors name their own blind spots. They filtered out places where water tables have fallen steadily for decades, often from heavy pumping, because a long decline makes single droughts hard to pick out. Those places may be underrepresented in the results.

Every number here is also a model’s estimate. This model performed well against real wells, but global groundwater models have both overestimated and underestimated water levels in the past.

And because the team averaged 60 years together, the results can’t show whether recovery is speeding up or slowing down.

“I want to dive deeper into how these recovery patterns have changed over time, as the current work has mainly focused on the spatial pattern,” Hauswirth said.

Next, the team wants to pair the four categories with projections of a warmer climate. That could show which places are at risk of shifting from resilient toward vulnerable or unstable.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Water.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6363. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6362. Semaglutide study raises new questions about pregnancy safety

A small sheep study found that semaglutide reduced maternal cardiac output, uterine blood flow, and fetal oxygen levels within two hours.

Semaglutide – the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy – can help people lose weight and reduce cardiovascular risk in certain patients.

Some women taking semaglutide will become pregnant before they know it.

Although human studies have examined pregnancy exposure, the potential effects on fetal development remain uncertain.

A new animal study from Adelaide University examines how a single dose affects maternal circulation and fetal oxygen levels in sheep.

Researchers gave a single dose of semaglutide to pregnant sheep and tracked what happened using phase-contrast MRI.

Within two hours, maternal cardiac output dropped significantly. Blood flow to the uterus fell with it. And oxygen levels in the fetal blood declined.

The study is small and preliminary – seven pregnant ewes, one acute dose. But the measurements are precise.

Researchers surgically catheterized the fetal femoral artery and the maternal jugular vein at 113–116 days of gestation.

They then performed MRI scans at 117–119 days to measure cardiac output and uterine artery blood flow at baseline, 20 minutes post-infusion, and two hours post-infusion. The dose was 0.75 mg of semaglutide.

Blood pressure didn’t change in the mothers or fetuses. Heart rates stayed steady.

But maternal cardiac output fell by 0.80 liters per minute at the two-hour mark compared to baseline.

Uterine blood flow remained the same proportion of maternal cardiac output, suggesting that its decline reflected the reduction in overall blood pumped by the mother’s heart.

Fetal oxygen levels told the rest of the story.

Partial pressure of oxygen in fetal arterial blood dropped from 23.25 mmHg at baseline to 19.94 at 45 minutes and 18.82 at two hours.

The decline from baseline was statistically significant at two hours.

“Within two hours of administering semaglutide, we found that the amount of blood pumped by the mother’s heart had significantly decreased, reducing blood flow to the uterus and lowering oxygen levels in the developing fetus,” said study co-author Mitchell Lock.

“Oxygen is essential for healthy fetal growth and development, so any reduction in its supply raises questions about what might happen if exposure to the drug continues throughout pregnancy.”

Those are acute effects from a single dose. This experiment did not assess the effects of repeated exposure.

Semaglutide is not recommended during pregnancy. Product labeling advises stopping semaglutide at least two months before a planned pregnancy.

That guidance assumes people plan their pregnancies – which, of course, many don’t.

A 2025 KFF poll found that 12% of US adults were currently taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss or other health conditions.

In Australia, around half a million people take them for diabetes alone, and the real number including off-label weight loss use is likely much higher.

Here’s the bind. Some women will be reluctant to stop because they don’t want to regain weight.

Others taking the drug for diabetes may worry about destabilizing their blood sugar management. And some will simply conceive before they realize they should have stopped.

“While weight-loss medications have become incredibly popular, there’s still a lot we don’t know about how they might affect a developing baby,” Lock said.

This is a sheep study that gave a single acute dose to seven animals. The results show what happens in the first two hours, not across an entire pregnancy.

The mechanism – reduced cardiac output leading to reduced uterine flow and fetal oxygenation – is plausible and physiologically coherent, but it hasn’t been demonstrated in humans.

“Our findings suggest a potential risk to fetal development, but we haven’t yet established whether these short-term changes affect fetal growth, what happens over a longer period of semaglutide use or whether similar effects could occur in human pregnancies,” said coauthor Janna Morrison.

“With the growing popularity of GLP-1 medications, it’s important that we better understand their potential effects during pregnancy so women and healthcare professionals can make informed and safe decisions about their use.”

The study doesn’t prove semaglutide harms human fetuses. It found that a single dose was followed by lower fetal arterial oxygen pressure in pregnant sheep.

The findings raise questions about whether repeated exposure could affect fetal growth and whether similar circulatory changes occur in humans.

Human pregnancy studies have not established a consistent increase in major birth defects following semaglutide exposure, but the available evidence remains limited.

This small sheep study adds a physiological finding that warrants further investigation.

The findings were reported in a conference abstract in the journal Heart, Lung and Circulation.

#6360. Tiny sparrows hold ancient clues to human heart disease

A detailed map of sparrow heart cells reveals similarities with human hearts and clues to how birds adapt to life at high altitude.

A tiny sparrow has more in common with us than you’d think – at least when it comes to the heart.

Scientists have built the first single-cell atlas of a wild bird’s heart, analyzing more than 200,000 cells and nuclei from newborn and adult Eurasian tree sparrows.

What they found is a remarkably conserved cardiac blueprint.

Similar core cell types, gene activity patterns, and disease-linked pathways – shared across species separated by 300 million years of evolution.

The study was led by researchers at the Institute of Zoology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Scientists compared heart cells from sparrows living at sea level in Cangzhou (10 meters altitude) and high on the Tibetan Plateau at Gahai (3,400 meters).

The team, led by Yan Hao, Xiang Zhou, and Qingshuo Zhao, sequenced 168,634 neonatal cells and 33,694 adult nuclei.

Eleven major cardiac cell types showed up in sparrow hearts. These include cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and immune cells.

That’s similar to what we find in mice and humans. But the proportions shift dramatically between life stages.

Cardiomyocytes, the heart’s muscle cells, accounted for 22% of the neonatal sample and 11% of the adult sample.

Endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, accounted for 13% of the neonatal sample and 31% of the adult sample.

The baby heart is built for rapid growth. The adult heart is built for endurance – a dense network to keep blood and oxygen flowing under sustained demand.

Using a computational tool called CAME, the researchers mapped sparrow heart cells against those of mice and humans. Matching rates ranged from 86.7% to 99.5%.

Cardiomyocytes were the most conserved cell type of all, with cross-species gene expression correlations between 0.57 and 0.62. That’s a tight overlap for animals that last shared an ancestor before dinosaurs went extinct.

Fibroblasts and endothelial cells were more species-specific, with human-sparrow correlations dropping to 0.23–0.24.

That makes biological sense. Heart muscle cells must meet strict demands for electrical signaling and contraction.

Supporting cells like fibroblasts have more freedom to adapt to each species’ particular mechanical environment.

The team didn’t stop at cataloging cell types. They asked whether the genes conserved across species also happen to be the ones that go wrong in human heart disease.

The answer was a strong yes. In adult hearts, genes linked to known human cardiac pathologies showed tight expression correlations between tree sparrows and both mice and humans.

The sparrow-human correlations (0.53 to 0.66) were statistically comparable to mouse-human correlations (0.52 to 0.72).

That’s a remarkable finding. The similarities suggest that sparrows could help researchers investigate biological pathways involved in human heart disease.

Sparrows living at 3,400 meters face a persistent shortage of oxygen, known as chronic hypoxia.

Their hearts are larger, with more blood vessels, a typical high-altitude adaptation.

At the cellular level, those adaptations diverge sharply by age. Adult high-altitude cardiomyocytes showed 191 differentially expressed genes, mostly tied to cardiac muscle development.

Neonatal ones showed only 22, focused instead on energy metabolism. Just two genes overlapped.

While baby hearts at altitude appear to prioritize energy metabolism under limited oxygen, adult hearts emphasize structural changes. So they respond to the same stressor differently depending on life stage.

Among the altitude-adaptation genes, one stood out: IGF1R. It encodes a receptor in the insulin-like growth factor pathway and sits at a hub connecting MAPK signaling, cytoskeletal organization, and cardiac muscle contraction.

It’s already known to drive heart enlargement in mice and humans. The researchers found it upregulated in high-elevation sparrow cardiomyocytes too.

To test whether it actually causes hypertrophy in birds, they overexpressed IGF1R in chicken cardiomyocyte cultures.

The cells grew significantly larger, with elevated levels of hypertrophy markers NPPA and ACTA1.

Gene activity changes were consistent with involvement of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway.

Growth-promoting genes like BDNF, BCL2, and MYC went up.

The study used different sequencing technologies for neonates and adults, which could introduce technical artifacts when comparing life stages.

The IGF1R experiments were done in cell culture, not living birds. So the gene is a plausible contributor to high-altitude heart growth, but not yet a confirmed driver in vivo.

And while the sparrow-human gene correlations are impressive, they were somewhat weaker in neonatal hearts. This suggests developmental trajectories diverge more than adult endpoints do.

The bigger picture is about what hearts share after 300 million years of going their separate evolutionary ways.

Birds and mammals independently evolved four-chambered hearts as well as endothermy. And now it turns out they built them with strikingly similar molecular machinery.

That shared regulatory logic means sparrows could become a useful model for human cardiovascular disease.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation Life.

#6358. Cat urine may hold an early warning of kidney disease

A protein in cat urine may help detect kidney disease earlier, while other protein patterns could reveal different types of damage.

Kidney disease is common in cats, but vets often find it late. The usual blood test may still look normal after a cat has lost more than a third of its kidney function.

Now, researchers have found a possible early warning sign in cat urine. A protein called MMP-7 was higher in cats at the earliest stage of the disease.

The study also found three groups of sick cats with different patterns of urine proteins. This suggests that cats with the same diagnosis may have different kinds of kidney damage.

Katelyn Brusach led the work in Jessica Quimby’s feline kidney research program at The Ohio State University College of Veterinary Medicine.

Her team compared urine from 30 healthy cats and 34 cats with chronic kidney disease, including just five at the earliest stage.

Estimates of how common chronic kidney disease, or CKD, is in cats vary widely. It is especially common in older cats.

CKD means the kidneys have lost some of their ability to work, and that loss lasts over time.

The damage can begin in the kidneys’ filters, their tiny tubes, or the tissue around them.

Vets usually measure creatinine in the blood to diagnose CKD and judge its stage. This substance comes from muscles, so when a sick cat loses muscle, the reading can look falsely low.

Creatinine and another blood marker called SDMA can reliably identify middle and late stages, the researchers wrote, but early disease is harder to spot.

Knowing exactly what kind of damage has occurred requires a kidney biopsy, which is not always possible.

Vets use substances in blood or urine as clues to disease. Researchers call these substances biomarkers.

“The search for more precise biomarkers is not unique to feline CKD,” Brusach said. “This is a common problem in biomarker discovery across other chronic diseases.”

Her team turned to urine because it comes directly from the kidneys. Changes in its proteins could offer clues about changes inside those organs.

All 64 cats in the study were pets enrolled during clinical exams at Ohio State. The cats with CKD had stable disease.

The researchers classified the sick cats using the International Renal Interest Society‘s four-stage system.

Five had stage one disease, 15 had stage two, eight had stage three, and six had stage four, the most severe.

They examined each urine sample with a mass spectrometer, a machine that identifies molecules by their mass. This let them look at many proteins at once.

The team identified 2,219 different proteins. As far as the researchers knew, no earlier study had used this method to identify so many proteins in cat urine.

The team first compared the five cats at stage one with the 30 healthy cats. Several proteins differed between the two groups.

Only MMP-7 also tracked creatinine levels across all 64 cats. Cats with higher creatinine, a sign that their kidneys were working less well, tended to have more MMP-7 in their urine.

MMP-7 is an enzyme that breaks down material around cells.

Researchers think its family of enzymes plays a role in kidney scarring, but they disagree about whether these enzymes add to scarring or help limit it.

An earlier study of cat kidneys found that genes for three enzymes in this family were more active in diseased tissue, but only MMP-7 was linked to creatinine.

Brusach’s team suggested that MMP-7 may offer an early sign of kidney scarring.

Kidney disease can look different from one cat to the next, making it hard for one protein to tell the whole story.

“Chronic diseases are often heterogeneous, which makes them challenging to encapsulate with one protein,” Brusach said.

The team compared the full mix of urine proteins from each cat. Healthy cats grouped together, but some cats with early CKD fell into that same group.

The researchers suggested that early disease may not yet change many urine proteins, or that standard tests missed disease in some apparently healthy cats.

Some cats initially classified as healthy later received a CKD diagnosis.

The remaining cats with CKD fell into three groups separate from the healthy cats. These groups offered possible clues to different kinds of damage.

One group included five cats: four with stage two disease and one with stage three. The researchers found no distinctive pattern of urine proteins in this group.

The researchers suggested that these cats might have a more stable form of the disease, might not yet have worsened, or might have normally aging kidneys.

Scientists still do not fully understand why some cats get worse while others do not. In a 2012 study cited by the team, 81% of cats at stage two did not reach stage four before they died.

A second group contained five younger male cats with advanced disease.

Their urine had higher levels of proteins involved in immune responses and blood clotting, and all five had excess protein in their urine.

The team suspected that the immune system was causing inflammation in the kidneys’ filters, an uncommon problem in cats.

Without biopsies, though, they could not confirm that explanation.

The third group included seven cats with high levels of a different set of proteins. Some of those proteins occur in the membranes around cells.

This pattern may point to damage in the cells lining the kidneys’ tiny tubes. The researchers suggested it could reflect the usual form of late-stage CKD.

The study included few cats at stage one or stage four and few elderly cats with healthy kidneys. Healthy cats averaged 6.4 years old, while cats with CKD averaged 11.3.

Age or sex may have influenced the groups, but the study was not designed to test either factor.

The researchers also cannot yet say how well MMP-7 or any of the protein patterns would work as a test.

The team called for future studies that directly measure the proteins it identified.

For MMP-7, a larger and more varied group of cats would help show whether it can reliably tell early disease apart from healthy kidneys.

Zoetis Inc. funded the work through a sponsored research agreement with Quimby’s lab.

The study is published in the Journal of Proteome Research.
