Annual passes to major U.S. theme parks like Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando Resort, SeaWorld and Legoland come with a long list of benefits. You can visit as often as you like; you get discounts on extras like parking, merchandise and dining; and your pass often comes with access to special events throughout the year.

Theme park annual passes also come with a hefty price tag that can climb upward of $1,000. Because of this, it can be easy to assume an annual pass is only worth the cost if you live near one of these parks and can visit every week.

As an out-of-state resident who has held an annual pass to Universal Orlando Resort since 2020, I can assure you that assumption is incorrect. But you don't have to take my word for it.

I calculated the break-even point for 10 theme parks across the country to help you decide whether it's an option worth looking into. For consistency, I based these calculations on each park's top-tier pass and the lowest one-day ticket prices, using park-to-park tickets at resorts with multiple parks, since annual passes include park-to-park access.

Because these calculations are based on one-day tickets, you would still need to determine whether you could save money with an annual pass by considering the ticket cost on the date(s) of your visit (most parks have variable pricing), how many trips you take each year and the number of days you visit per trip.

**About 6 once you factor in the cost of free parking and the Express passes

Disney World offers several annual passes, but only one, the Disney Incredi-Pass, is available to out-of-state residents. The Disney Incredi-Pass has no blockout dates and includes complimentary theme park parking.

If you were to visit only on the cheapest days of the year, you would need to visit nine times each year to realize the value of a Disney World annual pass as a non-Florida resident. When you factor in shopping and dining discounts and free parking, you can probably break even after eight visits. But if you were to visit on the more expensive days, you could break even in closer to six days.

Related: Bluey, Buzz and Grogu: Opening dates for new Disney World and Disneyland attractions in 2026

Remember, though, this comparison is based on the one-day ticket price. If you plan to spend eight days at Disney World broken up between one or two visits per year, you could potentially do better to buy a multiday park hopper ticket versus an annual pass. Because Disney uses variable ticket pricing and tickets get less expensive as you add more days, you have to do the math to find out which is best for you.

Don't worry, the math on most other parks isn't quite as involved.

Disneyland's top-tier pass is called the Inspire Key. At $1,899 per year, this pass has blackout dates during the weeks of Christmas and New Year's Eve, and it includes free standard parking and unlimited Disney PhotoPass downloads.

The Inspire Key pass can pay for itself after 11 visits, since the lowest park hopper tickets start at $179.

Related: How Disneyland's newest ride proves that 'progress is impossible without change'

As with Disney World, the number of visits required to break even would decrease if you visited on more expensive days, and you could still save money by purchasing multiday tickets.

Universal Orlando has several annual pass options, but the 2-Park Premier Pass is the easiest to use and has the most benefits. You get park-to-park admission between Universal Studios Florida and Universal Islands of Adventure, complimentary skip-the-line Express passes after 4 p.m., complimentary valet and prime parking, one free ticket to Halloween Horror Nights, early park admission and several valuable discounts.

If you were to visit during the holidays when one-day park-to-park tickets climb as high as $255, you can break even after four days. It's also worth doing the calculations with the included Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $99. When you factor that in, you can break even after five visits.

Related: Epic Universe tips: 11 ways to spend less time in line and have more fun

A six-day park-to-park ticket that also includes access to Universal Epic Universe is only $550.99 per person, so if you only plan to visit once per year for six days, you would save significantly by purchasing a multiday ticket versus an annual pass.

Universal Studios Hollywood only has one park, making the math here easier to calculate. The park's Platinum Annual Pass has no blockout dates and includes free general parking most of the year, one Halloween Horror Nights ticket and Express skip-the-line access after 3 p.m.

You'd technically have to visit 6.0025 times to break even, but if you include the free parking and after-3 p.m. Express passes, we can safely say you break even after six visits.

Related: Thrills for all ages: 6 best rides at Universal Studios Hollywood

Similar to Universal Orlando, you can break even sooner if you factor in the cost of a Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $77 per person. When you factor that in, plus those other perks, you can break even after approximately five one-day visits.

This is where things get a little bit fun (in my opinion, anyway). Legoland's Premium Annual Pass includes visits to more than 20 Merlin attractions across the country, including Legoland, Peppa Pig Park, Sea Life Aquarium, Madame Tussauds wax museum and more. A lot of these parks are in theme park hubs like Florida, California and Texas, so you likely aren't too far from one or multiple locations.

In this case, you don't need to plan multiple visits to a single park to see the value in an annual pass. You can visit multiple locations around the country with no blockout dates, free parking and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets (one ticket per quarter), which make the math very appealing.

If you assign a $69 value to the "Bring-A-Friend" tickets, four per year would equal $276, just $23 less than the total annual pass cost. So, if you were to visit one of the 20+ parks nationwide four times per year (once per quarter) and bring a friend or family member with you, you'd save money with an annual pass before even factoring in free parking and other discounts.

This is another instance where you can access multiple parks with a single annual pass. SeaWorld Orlando's Platinum Pass includes unlimited admission to 11 parks across the country with no blockout dates. These include all SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks, as well as their affiliated water parks. You also get eight free guest tickets, free photos and free preferred parking.

A few notes here. You can't use all eight free guest tickets at the same time and they are limited to select parks. SeaWorld allows you to use a certain number of tickets during different calendar windows throughout the year. But if you were to visit these parks eight times per year and bring a friend, you would save more than $600 by purchasing an annual pass.

It's also worth noting that SeaWorld San Diego's Platinum Pass is only $201 on sale, and its lowest one-day ticket costs $64.99, so you'd break even after just four visits. While it provides the passholder access to the same 11 parks, its guest passes can only be used at the California parks.

Opened in July 2026, Universal Kids Resort is the newest park on this list. The park recently started selling annual passes, with the Gold Annual Pass being its top-tier offering. The Gold pass has no blockout dates and includes regular self-parking.

Assuming you visit on five separate days and only visit on the least expensive days, you would break even after five visits. But because the Gold Pass also includes free parking and other discounts, you could potentially break even in four one-day visits. Because the park also sells discounted multiday tickets, the above math only makes sense if you were to visit on five nonconsecutive days.

You don't need to live in Florida or California to have access to award-winning theme parks. Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, consistently wins awards for its cleanliness, water park and thrilling coasters. Holiday World's Platinum Pass has no blockout dates, early entry for select attractions and discounted "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Holiday World already offers free parking, sunscreen and soft drinks, so you won't get additional discounts there. You would break even after four one-day visits, assuming you purchase the lowest-cost tickets.

Dollywood's top-of-the-line pass is a Diamond Season Pass (a very fitting name for our bright and shining queen Dolly Parton, if you ask me). With it, you get unlimited visits, complimentary parking, Time Saver skip-the-line access for the first hour of each day, a 20% discount on shopping and dining, and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Dollywood handles its "Bring-a-Friend" tickets differently. You can use them one at a time or all four at once. If you brought four friends with you during your first visit after buying your annual pass, you would have more than covered the cost of your pass. In fact, you could save about $110 by purchasing an annual pass instead of five one-day tickets (you and four friends). Any future visits that year are just a bonus. Just one of the million reasons to love Dollywood.

Silver Dollar City and Dollywood are owned by the same parent company (Herschend Family Entertainment), but their annual passes work quite differently. Silver Dollar City's Diamond Pass includes unlimited visits to the park and White Water water park, eight free "Bring A Friend" tickets (to be used during specific redemption windows at Silver Dollar City or White Water), a bonus "Bring-a-Friend" ticket you can use on any day and $29.99 tickets for friends and family.

Even though you can't use all of your "Bring-a-Friend" tickets at one time, you only need to visit with a guest twice to break even with an annual pass before even digging into the savings you would find from in-park discounts.

In addition to the advertised benefits, there is a level of convenience that comes with being a passholder. You can pop in for a few hours without feeling like you wasted money on a full-day ticket, and you feel like a more valuable guest when you visit. I often get things like priority parade seating, fun freebies and passholder-only discounts of up to 70% off merchandise.

No amount of math matters unless you know you will actually use and enjoy the benefits of being a passholder. Use these calculations as a jumping-off point to decide if you are ready to be a passholder.

#6244. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6243. American Airlines Makes Hotel Vouchers Easier To Get, But Warns Of Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how it provides hotel rooms, food credits, and transportation to passengers stranded by flight disruptions. Getting help without standing in another long line is welcome. But an internal memo also warns that employees may have fewer hotel choices to offer, which leaves me wondering whether a faster voucher will necessarily mean a better night.

View From The Wing highlights a November employee memo outlining changes to American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, known internally as HMT.

American was already promoting automatic disruption vouchers in 2025. The question now is whether the latest changes make that assistance more reliable and easier to use.

I recently wrote about my American Airlines flight from Chicago to Los Angeles that nearly became an overnight stay.

A 7:10 p.m. departure slipped repeatedly until the posted departure time reached 11:55 p.m. The aircraft was there, but we had no pilots. Eventually, pilots arrived from Dallas and received a chorus of cheers from passengers who were thrilled we might actually get home.

During the wait, an Admirals Club agent offered me a hotel room if I wanted to rebook for the next day. The offer came with a caveat:

I appreciated having an option, but I wanted to get to Los Angeles. By that point, an airport hotel would have meant a short night followed by another trip through security and another flight.

But it is a reason why I appreciate this new rollout. Every minute spent waiting for an agent to arrange accommodation is a minute you cannot spend sleeping. If American can deliver a usable hotel offer to your phone promptly, that is a practical improvement.

“Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing.”

Yes, a shorter list of suitable properties could work perfectly well and it is too early to say whether the remaining hotel options will be worse. But I’m not all that optimistic, here.

What happens when the available hotel is far from the airport, has no functioning shuttle at that hour, or cannot accommodate a family in an appropriate room.

We are not talking about putting every stranded passenger in a luxury hotel. But I do expect a clean room and a workable way to get there and back. A voucher is useful only if the accommodation behind it is suitable.

My agent’s Hilton comment was amusing, but it also captured the uncertainty. When you accept an airline-arranged room late at night, you may have little idea what you are getting.

Uber Central allows businesses to request rides for customers who do not have the Uber app. Riders receive trip details and a tracking link by text.

That could be particularly helpful for someone who rarely uses rideshare services or is already overwhelmed by a disrupted journey.

According to the reported instructions, however, hotel shuttles remain the first option, followed by Uber vouchers. Agent-arranged rides are intended for exceptions when those options do not meet the passenger’s needs. Broad availability of the new arrangement has not yet been established.

I hope agents have enough discretion to solve the actual problem. A hotel shuttle listed in a database is no help if it stopped running an hour ago…as a practical aside, before you leave the airport terminal call the hotel to make sure that the shuttle is running.

Under American’s published customer service plan, when a disruption is caused by the airline, assistance available upon request includes:

The plan also promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs if American cannot provide an approved hotel voucher (with an almost impossible caveat that such authorization must be obtained in writing). For disruptions beyond its control, such as weather, American generally leaves passengers responsible for their own accommodation and meals.

If you qualify for assistance and no automatic offer arrives, ask an agent. And if you get the food/beverage voucher, realize that the $12 won’t go very far (unless you are in Denver).

American Airlines deserves credit for making disruption assistance easier to deliver. Passengers who have already lost hours to a delay should not have to lose another hour obtaining a hotel voucher.

But fewer hotel choices could limit the usefulness of that improvement. I will judge the system by whether it gets stranded passengers into suitable rooms promptly, with transportation that actually works.

On my recent Chicago flight, I was thankful the pilots arrived and I never needed the hotel. Next time, I may not be so fortunate…(or maybe next time I will fly Delta or United).

#6242. 10 Spacious Villas in Morocco Fit for a Relaxing Group Getaway

The bustling capital city has perennial charm, but beyond its walls, there’s so much more to Morocco worth exploring. Whether you’re gearing up for a hiking trip to the Atlas mountains, looking to immerse yourself in the sights and sounds of the buzzy souks or headed out to the coast, there’s a fantastic nearby address to know. Most of our favorite Morocco villas pair idyllic views with in-house chefs, housekeepers, and even security staff for a hotel-worthy break in your own space. Below are 10 of the best villas in Morocco to rent for your next trip.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost or Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Bed & bath: 5 bedrooms, 5 bathroomsTop amenities: Heated pool, home cinema, sauna and steam room

This is the kind of holiday home that keeps everyone happy, making it perfect for a large family with different ideas of what a great holiday looks like. The interiors are modern, but Moroccan charm is preserved in the details. The five spacious bedrooms all feature en suite bathrooms and are spread across both floors. The large living area, with its circular arrangement of comfortable sofas, and the home cinema invite guests to relax and enjoy each other's company during their stay. A fitness center and a traditional hammam add a wellness touch to the home. There is a golf course right next door, should you fancy a round of golf.

Bed & bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathroomsTop amenities: Pool, hammam, pickleball court, pétanque, barbecue

Located just north of Marrakech, this villa gives groups a soft, quiet place to land after a busy day in the city—and plenty of activities to keep everyone busy on days spent on-site. Beyond the resort-style heated swimming pool lined with lounge chairs, the pétanque and pickleball courts encourage some healthy competition. Afterwards, spend a bit of relaxation time in the hammam or massage room, or kick back in the garden. Of note, two of the eight bedrooms are located in an annex of the villa and share a bathroom.

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 6 bathroomsTop amenities: Heated pool, outdoor dining space

To reach this villa, you have to drive 30 minutes from Marrakech into the stunning Ourika Valley. On arrival, you’ll immediately notice the snow-capped peaks of the Atlas Mountains rising around the property. The 8,000-square-meter garden dotted with olive trees and cacti is the perfect setting for days spent lying by the large pool, playing pétanque, or cooking up a storm with produce from the organic kitchen garden. Inside, the house is bathed in sunlight and particularly stunning at dawn. There are six bedrooms, all featuring en suite bathrooms for ultimate comfort. Five of the bedrooms are in the main house—as well as the kitchen and the spacious living room featuring a dining space with a fireplace—while the final bedroom is in the annex, alongside the playroom and wellness area with a hammam.

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 6 bathsTop amenities: Terrace, pool, hot tub, gym

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 7 bathsTop amenities: Pool, terraces, Atlas Mountains views

Palais Les Orchidées is a palace-like six-suite villa just outside the center of Marrakech, combining grand architecture with pared-back interiors and views towards the Atlas Mountains. The property is surrounded by leafy gardens, with a large swimming pool and several terraces providing plenty of space to relax outdoors. Inside, all six suites have king-size beds and en suite bathrooms with bathtubs and showers, making this a particularly comfortable option for a large group or several couples traveling together. Despite its peaceful setting, you won’t be too far from the action: the villa is around 15 minutes by car from some of Marrakech’s best-known sights, including the Koutoubia, Bahia Palace, and Jardin Majorelle, and around 20 minutes from Marrakech Menara Airport. Breakfast can also be served at the villa for an additional charge.

Bed & bath: 5 bedrooms, 5 bathsTop amenities: Rooftop terrace, private pool, breakfast chef

This classic Marrakech riad is a bohemian dream with vibrant, patterned tiles, a mishmash of colorful, soft furnishings, and a beautiful outdoor courtyard—bringing good vibes only. You’ll be well taken care of here; daily housekeeping, a breakfast chef, and a night guard will ensure everything goes swimmingly. Take an alfresco lunch before a dip in the plunge pool, then settle on the daybed for a leisurely afternoon with a view—there’s a panoramic vista of both the buzzing medina and the Atlas mountain range. Take note: You’ll have to climb some steps to reach this villa, and there’s no parking outside, so if you’re taking a car, you’ll need to leave it a short distance away. However, there are a slew of excellent restaurants and hammams within walking distance and good public transport links right outside.

Bed & bath: 9 bedrooms, 9 bathsTop amenities: Outdoor kitchen, sauna/steam room, gym

Like most experiences in Morocco, stepping into this palatial villa’s vast grounds is a sensory feast from the get-go. Plaster pink walls, an eclectic mix of bright furniture, ornate artwork, patterned rugs, and glittering chandeliers are wrapped around the central turquoise jewel of the outdoor pool. It has nine huge bedrooms, at least one of which has a statement roll-top tub in the corner, plus nine bathrooms—so no waiting in line for the shower here. It’s a great choice for bachelor or bachelorette parties and big group getaways, with multiple comfy gathering spaces for catch-ups with a view. First, head to the meeting room to grab a drink from the bar, but take them to the rooftop terrace to maximize the experience—the views at sunset are fantastic. Extra bookable spa and hammam treatments make a stay in this Moroccan palace all the sweeter.

Bed & bath: 8 bedrooms, 8 bathsTop amenities: Private pool, courtyard, outdoor shower, record player

This isn’t a riad, but a former fondouk—a 19th-century inn that used to accommodate travelers before they set sail on trading voyages. Now, however, it has been transformed into a chic villa for 15, set around four distinct courtyard spaces decorated with fragrant lemon trees and mature prickly cacti. Locally sourced clay walls bring traditional flair that keeps you cool on hot Moroccan nights, and there’s a pool to jump into for welcome midday dips. Active types, take note. This villa sits in the ancient walled city of Taraudant, which offers easy access to both the High Access and Anti-Atlas hiking routes. It's the perfect place to wind down after a long day of mountain treks.

Bed & bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsTop amenities: Terrace, courtyard, fireplace, private cook

Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsTop amenities: Private chefs, private heated pool, terrace

With a hilltop location looking down onto sparkling sea views, even by Moroccan standards, the views here are unbeatable. A clever design means the home provides ample opportunity to totally immerse yourself in the landscape. Run a bath in the outdoor tub right on the beachfront, and awake to sunrise light streaming through floor-to-ceiling windows framing gentle ocean waves. Mealtimes are sorted thanks to the in-house private chefs who’ll cook up anything you please to be enjoyed alfresco with a glass of wine on the terrace next to the private heated pool. There’s a slew of activities on offer in Essaouira—tell the hosts what you’d like to do and they’ll make it happen.

#6241. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6240. How to Spend a Rainy Day in New York City

A rainy day in New York City is no new phenomenon, but that doesn’t make its occurrence any less disappointing. According to reporting from News 12, Central Park only reported nine completely dry weekends out of the past 40 weekends of 2026, putting a real—forgive me—damper on park hangs and beach days. In case you count yourself among the masses with foiled plans, we at Condé Nast Traveler have you covered. Our editors have weathered their fair share of cold and dreary days in the city and learned to love the rain. After all, it’s the best excuse to dry off by the crackling fireplace of a plush hotel lobby, or conversely, to take a dip into the steaming Russian Turkish baths to cure the sinking cold. Instead of willing the clouds to part, bear your galoshes and head to our editors’ favorite things to do in New York City on a rainy day.

That travel editors love a hotel lobby is about as unsurprising as a dad joke, but there’s nothing like a mini staycation to salvage a lost weekend. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is partial to The Hotel Chelsea. The neighborhood institution has moved far past its roach-ridden days when Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe were Just Kids, and the experience of their lobby is the apotheosis of that evolution. There’s a lot of modern polish, sure, but all the charming verdigris has been kept intact. There’s the art from the hotel’s most (in)famous guests splashed over the walls, the wrought iron chandeliers bathing the space in romantic lighting, and the aforementioned fireplace tying a bow around the mood. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that the hotel’s Lobby Bar is just right next door. If Chelsea feels like a slog to commute to, there are plenty of great options scattered across the map, from the Ace Hotel Brooklyn which has plenty of public workspaces, or Times Square’s Algonquin Hotel, which saw the genesis of The New Yorker just 100 years ago.

The easiest remedy for rainy day restlessness is to stretch your legs at one of the city’s finest museums, though even the impressive 2.2 million-square-foot expanse of the Met becomes easily dwarfed when you’re crammed in by a surge of fellow museum-goers who had the exact same idea. Instead, spend your day exploring NYC’s smaller scholarly corners. Editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez heads to East Williamsburg art organization Amant whenever she feels like she’s cooped inside her apartment, watching the hours just slip away. To start, there’s no need to worry about ponying up big ticket prices as entry is always free. “Peruse the titles at Kis Café and Bookstore, then head to gallery spaces 932 Grand and 315 Maujer; across the street, you’ll find multimedia installations in Géza,” says Alvarez, “The exhibit Sentient Earth currently spans all three galleries, bringing together 28 artists to examine the ways we’ve impacted the planet (and what—if it gained sentience—its response to us might be). Do explore Amant's event programming of screenings and panels, which you can find here.” Other small but mighty options include the Financial District’s public poetry library Poets House, which overlooks the Hudson and Bushwick’s Bone Museum, which also houses resident tuxedo cat Bone Jovi.

Film critic Anthony Lane once posited, “as a rough rule, cinema can be sundered into two halves: six-o’clock films and nine-o’clock films,” and a rainy day is certainly the occasion for the six-o’clock variety and all its ritual: rallying a group to go with, booking the early dinner reservation, whiling away at a nearby bar after to unpack what you’ve just seen. Commerce director Madison Flager likes the Lincoln Center AMC, home to the largest IMAX screen in the country, clocking in at 75.6 feet tall by 101 feet wide, which is roughly the size of a 10-story building. News editor Hannah Towey, on the other hand, dodges the rain at the Metrograph, a boutique two-screen theater keeping the spirit of Prohibition-era New York alive and well. Whichever way you lean, you can always count on NYC’s trusty movie theaters to show you something new.

The less-than-stellar weather shouldn’t keep you from embarking on a treasure hunt, and doing your due diligence enclosed inside one of the city’s coolest vintage stores is a surefire way to uncover a few gems. Alvarez recommends the Flatiron District’s Surrender Dorothy, where the racks are piled with the well-loved and pristine, collector’s items and forgotten blasts from the past, avant-garde art pieces, and buy-it-for-life workwear. It’s dopamine dressing at its best. You could also try your luck at one of the city’s larger franchises like Beacon’s Closet, or, if you’re willing to face the elements, dive into a flea market.

One of the best spots to people-watch in the city, come rain or shine, is the baths. And having a place to hide from the chill and unforgiving precipitation is a welcome bonus. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima touts the East Village’s Russian Turkish Baths as the perfect place to drop by. Melt away whatever’s ailing you in the 215 °F Russian Sauna, and if you need any help doing so, get the platza oak leaf ritual where spa employees forcefully smack your pores open with bushels of oak leaves in the sauna. If you’re looking for something a little more communal, Flager likes to warm up at Othership, which sets itself apart with its guided wellness experiences that combine breath work, aromatherapy, visualizations, somatic movement, live music, and group “shares.”

Nothing brings a bar together like its pool table, but if you’ve spent more time watching the queue of quarters waiting for your turn than the game itself, head to a dedicated pool hall instead, where there’s a better chance of scoring a table all your own and watching the real pros practice their hand. Union Square’s Amsterdam Billiards has been a staple ever since I came to the city five years ago. The 11,000-square-foot hall decked with its array of Brunswick tables might seem intimidating at first, but take it from a real amateur: they may be serious about their snooker here, but they’re not snobby. Pool aside, patrons keep occupied with the hall’s other offerings like table tennis, beer pong, and darts. If you’re serious about upping your game, you can even book one-hour lessons with their in-house pros.

Jazz is one of the country’s greatest art forms, and New York is the genre’s most inspiring muse and resourceful studio. The city cemented its status in the 1920s Harlem Renaissance when legendary venues like the Cotton Club and Small’s Paradise put Duke Ellington, Fats Waller, and Billie Holiday in the national consciousness. Jazz in the city has traveled beyond its uptown crucible, and there’s great clubs peppered throughout the boroughs. Some of our favorites include Ornithology Jazz Club, which also has a killer vegan menu; Funny Bar, which comes from the same team as Baby’s All Right; and Greenwich Village’s Smalls Jazz Club, which keeps things true to form and no-frills.

New York’s historic theatre scene is far from confined to Broadway’s flashing lights. Some of the most exciting, intimate, and interactive productions in the city are playing Off-Broadway. Big names like Andrew Lloyd Webber have found a second wind in shows like Masquerade, a roving retelling of Phantom of the Opera, and fresh concepts like Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody are attracting their own audiences with their lower budget, DIY charm. Shows like these are a trove of talent, and odds are you can find one where you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg for entry at venues like La MaMa or Signature Theatre.

Associate social media manager Bridget Knowles swears by the people's princess of a dive bar as a haven from the harsh weather: “Interjecting here with what I’m sure we’re all thinking. I mean, sheesh. This is unspoken. A great dive bar is an oasis in New York City on a rainy day: a grunge mecca, a throw-some-hours-away swan song. My kind of place. A healthy dose of grime on an already lyrically imposing, moody day is great for the soul. Even if you’re off the Miller High Life (ah, it hurt to type, but pun intended) one of the greatest pastimes in life, according to me, is to simply load up touch tunes and shoot at a table a bit. Make some friends, watch something insane playing on a corner TV. You know, commiserate. Get your hands on some of the best in the city here.”

#6239. Southwest Airlines Offers “Free” Same-Day Flight Changes, But There’s A Seat-Fee Trap

Southwest Airlines offers eligible passengers free same-day flight changes, but there is a catch if you paid separately for your seat. Asking an airport agent to make the change can leave that seat purchase nonrefundable, while making the change through the app, website, or telephone receives different treatment. Apparently, how you change your flight now matters almost as much as which flight you choose.

View From The Wing highlights a peculiar provision in Southwest’s seat refund and exchange policy.

For passengers who separately purchased a seat on their original flight, Southwest explicitly states:

“Same-day change requested at the airport: Seat purchased on original flight is non-refundable.”

But complete that same-day change through Southwest.com, the Southwest app, or by telephone, and the rules provide a way to apply the original seat payment toward a replacement or receive a refund when buying a more expensive seat.

You could be standing at the gate with your phone in hand, looking at an earlier departure. Whether you tap the screen or ask the employee in front of you for help could affect what happens to money you already spent.

The policy concerns seats purchased separately from the airfare. Here is how Southwest describes the treatment when you voluntarily switch flights:

For a hypothetical example, suppose you paid $40 for a seat and make a confirmed same-day change through the app. If the replacement seat costs $30, Southwest applies the original payment but does not return the $10 difference.

If the replacement costs $50, you pay $50 upfront and generally receive a separate $40 refund. You should therefore check that the refund actually arrives rather than assuming the system simply charged you the difference.

Under Southwest’s same-day change policy, the confirmed-change benefit is available with Choice, Choice Preferred, and Choice Extra fares, along with Getaways by Southwest vacation bookings.

You need an available seat on a flight between the same origin and destination airports on the same travel date. The change must occur at least 10 minutes before your original scheduled departure.

Basic passengers must upgrade to an eligible fare first (and A-List or A-List Preferred status alone does not make a Basic ticket eligible for a free confirmed same-day change)

So when it comes to standby, there are two separate things to check: whether you can switch flights without an additional airfare charge, and what happens to the seat you purchased.

Do not confuse a confirmed change with same-day standby.

A confirmed change secures your place on the replacement flight immediately. Standby means waiting for space to become available, often much closer to boarding or even after boarding commences if you are waiting for no-shows. Southwest’s seat policy says the original seat purchase becomes nonrefundable when standby clears, regardless of how you joined the list.

Using the app therefore does not solve the seat-payment issue for standby. The eligibility rules differ too. A-List and A-List Preferred members can qualify for standby on Basic fares, even though those fares do not qualify for free confirmed same-day changes.

Of course, switching flights does not guarantee the same seat. Someone who bought extra legroom on one departure cannot reasonably expect an identical seat to materialize on a replacement flight. But why should the channel used to request the change determine the treatment of the original payment?

If Southwest can apply or refund that purchase when I use its app, why should asking an airport employee produce a less favorable rule? There may be a systems explanation, but that does little for a passenger who reasonably assumes an agent can provide the same options available online. On the other hand, I would bet that an agent who assigns you a superior seat in these sorts of situations is not going to charge for it…any frequent Southwest travelers want to weigh in?

This also puts employees in an awkward position. A passenger asks for help, receives it, then discovers that handling the transaction another way could have preserved the value of a seat purchase. For an airline that built so much goodwill around simplicity, this seems like an unnecessarily complicated way to handle a relatively ordinary request.

If you paid separately for a Southwest seat and want to make a confirmed same-day flight change, check the app or website before asking an airport agent to process it. Telephone changes also receive the more favorable treatment outlined in the policy.

Compare the replacement seat cost and keep track of any refund due. If you are using standby, remember that the app does not preserve the refundability of your original seat purchase once you clear.

A free flight change can still have consequences for the extras you purchased. Southwest passengers now have another reason to read the fine print before accepting what sounds like a straightforward benefit.

At The Points Guy, we’re always looking for simple ways to save money and earn more rewards. One of the easiest yet often overlooked tools is Chase Offers.

With just a few clicks, you can unlock targeted discounts and cash-back deals at brands you already use. These range from streaming services and restaurants to travel and retail purchases.

Even better, Chase Offers can often be combined with your card’s usual earning rates and shopping portals, helping you get more value from everyday spending.

Here’s how the program works and how to maximize it.

Chase Offers is a program available on eligible Chase debit and credit cards that gives cardholders access to targeted deals, similar to Amex Offers. These offers typically provide cash back or a percentage back as a statement credit when you make a qualifying purchase.

Like similar programs from other issuers, offers are personalized. That means the deals you see may differ from what someone else receives. You may also see different offers across your own Chase cards.

Most Chase-issued consumer and business credit and debit cards are eligible for Chase Offers if the primary cardholder has a U.S. address listed as their primary residence or place of business.

To see if Chase Offers is available for your card, check your Chase mobile app or log in at Chase's website.

For Chase credit cards, primary cardholders and authorized officers can view and add offers. Authorized users and employees can't add offers themselves, but they can redeem offers that have already been added to the account.

Some of the most popular eligible cards include:

Chase Offers are also available on many cobranded Chase credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and select United Airlines and Marriott Bonvoy cards.

Each card may offer different deals, so it's worth checking all your accounts if you hold more than one Chase card.

You can find available offers on the Chase website and on the Chase app. To view your available offers on the website, log in to your account and find "Chase Offers" on the right-hand panel.

Alternatively, you can click on "Benefits & travel" on the top panel and select "Chase Offers", as shown below. Note that the offers shown below may not be available to you.

To view your Chase Offers on the Chase mobile app, log in to your account and then scroll down toward the middle of the main account dashboard. You should see a section titled “Chase Offers” showing some of your current offers.

Either the website or app option will bring you to the offers currently available for you to browse.

Offerings change daily and typically feature various types of goods and services. You may see deals for:

Offers typically range from about 5% to 30% back or provide a fixed statement credit after meeting a spending requirement. For example, you might receive a $20 statement credit after spending $100 with a specific merchant.

Chase Offers can be an easy way to save on purchases you’re already making, which is something TPG staffers have seen firsthand across a range of everyday spending.

TPG travel writer Rachel Craft, for example, recently used an offer on her for 15% back at home improvement stores. She bundled supplies for a few projects she already had planned into a single purchase and received $33 back. Meanwhile, TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson earned an $85 statement credit on a DISH Network purchase using his World of Hyatt card.

TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen has also had success with Chase Offers. He recently earned $15.81 back on Trans-Siberian Orchestra tickets purchased through SeatGeek with his Chase Freedom Flex. Since the purchase also fell within one of the card's Q3 rotating quarterly bonus categories, he earned 5% cash back on top of his Chase Offer savings (on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter, activation required).

And in an even bigger example of how these savings can add up, Nick earned a $125 statement credit through a Chase Offer on an IHG hotel stay booked through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, using his . By combining that offer with the card's The Edit and select hotels credits, he saved a total of $625 on the stay.

While individual savings may vary, these examples highlight how these targeted offers can add up, especially on purchases you already planned to make.

While you don’t have to enroll your card to start using the Chase Offers program, you do have to add each individual offer to your credit card. Adding them is easy — all you have to do is navigate to Chase Offers either online or through the Chase Mobile app and click “Add to card” on any available offer that interests you.

Alternatively, if you have a subscription to a service like MaxRewards Gold, your offers should be automatically activated for all linked cards.

Then, use your card at the specific merchant, and you should see a statement credit applied to your account within 30 days after your qualifying transaction posts, unless the offer terms state otherwise.

Once you arrive on the Chase Offers landing page, adding an offer to your account is very simple.

If you have multiple eligible Chase cards, you’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen. Note that if you have multiple sign-ins with Chase, such as one for your personal cards and one for business credit cards, you will only see cards associated with the account for which you’re currently signed in.

Again, note that the offers you see here may not be available for you.

Click on any offer to add it to your card. Then, use your card at the specific merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

Once you find an offer you would like to use in the app, the process is similar to the website process.

You can click on “See all available deals” to see the rest of your offers. You’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen if you have multiple eligible Chase cards.

Click on any offers to add them to your card, use your card at the participating merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

When you add an offer for a specific card, you must use that same card to redeem the offer. For example, if you add a Chase Offer to your , you must use that card to redeem that offer successfully.

Be sure to read the terms and conditions for each offer carefully. You only have a certain amount of time to use each offer, and many come with maximum earning limits. As long as you make your purchase by the expiration date, you should receive the credit even if the transaction posts after the expiration date.

Chase Offers are rewarded as a statement credit, even if you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points on regular spending.

One of the common threads among all Chase Offers is this condition: Payment must be made directly with the merchant. While you can still use services like mobile wallets and PayPal with Chase Offers, you can’t use third-party providers to make purchases.

Finally, Chase Offers are only available on eligible U.S.-issued Chase credit cards tied to U.S.-based accounts. However, some offers may still be valid at international merchants, particularly global brands like hotel chains, as long as the transaction is processed by the eligible merchant and charged to your enrolled card.

Since new offers are constantly added, it’s a good idea to go through your Chase Offers at least biweekly to review and add new offers. It doesn’t cost anything to add an offer and then not use it, so you can be pretty lenient with which offers you add.

If there’s even a tiny possibility that you’ll use an offer, you might as well add it to your card. If you use it, great; if not, it’s not a problem.

Chase Offers become significantly more valuable when you stack them with other rewards opportunities. This means combining an offer with a shopping portal and a credit card bonus category to earn multiple layers of rewards on the same purchase.

For example, imagine you’re booking a $200 stay at a Hyatt property. You could:

In this scenario, you’d earn 1,000 points through the portal, $10 cash back from your Freedom Flex and a $20 statement credit from the Chase Offer.

Instead of earning rewards from just one source, you’ve effectively tripled up on the same purchase.

Chase Offers are best used for purchases you were already planning to make. Like any coupon or sale, saving 10% on something you didn’t need isn’t actually saving money. But when used strategically, especially in combination with shopping portals and bonus categories, they can meaningfully boost your overall return.

By checking your offers regularly and combining them with bonus categories and shopping portals, you can turn everyday spending into meaningful savings over time.

#6237. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6236. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6235. 9 All-Inclusive Resorts in Cancún That Go Way Beyond an Open Bar

I first arrived in Cancún, Mexico, more than 20 years ago. I had big hair, pencil-thin eyebrows, and limited expectations for an all-inclusive vacation: A swim-up bar serving frozen margaritas was about all I needed. Since then, my priorities have shifted, and thankfully, Cancún’s all-inclusive resorts have grown up alongside me.

After two decades of return visits made easier by an abundance of nonstop US flights, I’ve become more discerning about what deserves a place in that up-front price. I’ve also discovered that Cancún’s enduring spring break reputation tells an incomplete story about what's on offer. Choose the right resort, and you can have a butler draw your evening bath, a private pool overlooking the Caribbean, and à la carte restaurants you’ll look forward to all afternoon, whether you prefer the Hotel Zone’s long sweep of white sand, the relative quiet of Playa Mujeres, or a boat ride out to Isla Mujeres.

The frozen margaritas are still here. But now, there’s much more worth checking in for. Read on for the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún worth planning a vacation around.

Mexican art gives this Playa Mujeres resort its personality. Rubén Soto’s concrete mural depicts native wildlife amid geometric patterns, while suites carry the aesthetic through warm woods and marble rather than tropical clichés. At Atelier, which welcomes ages 16+, you might have lunch overlooking the water at El Suspiro, then enjoy a pre-dinner mezcal cocktail at Bar de la Calle. Back in your suite, a rolling minibar holds wine and gourmet snacks, and room service answers around the clock. Most dining and premium spirits are included, though María Dolores by Edgar Núñez warrants a separate reservation—and budget—for its contemporary Mexican menu. Book an Inspira suite, and a butler can arrange your dinner reservations while you spend the afternoon at the rooftop infinity pool.

At Le Blanc, the pampering begins before you’ve unpacked—and your butler can handle that, too. Once you’re settled, the day’s agenda might amount to a poolside cocktail, a soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy pools, and deciding what to wear to dinner. This adults-only Hotel Zone retreat pairs pale interiors and Caribbean frontage with an unusually generous all-inclusive package: À la carte dining, premium drinks, 24-hour room service, and access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit are all included. Dinner might mean a French tasting menu at the esteemed Lumière or Italian cooking at Blanc Italia. Massages cost extra, but the daily chance to steam, soak, and unwind in the spa does not.

Two beaches are better than one, especially when they come with a lighthouse and Caribbean views in nearly every direction. Perched on the tip of Punta Cancún, Hyatt Ziva makes the most of its peninsula setting, with room for both family playtime and grown-up downtime. Little ones can race down waterslides and splash beneath fountains, while teenagers claim their own turf over billiards and foosball in the teens' lounge. For those whose idea of vacation involves neither, Turquoize (a tower within the resort) offers an adults-only escape with ocean-facing suites, butlers just a WhatsApp message away, and a rooftop infinity pool blissfully removed from the splash zone.

Behind Paradisus’s five glass-topped pyramids, one of Cancún’s most recognizable silhouettes, vines cascade through a soaring atrium, fountains burble below, and newly redesigned rooms turn beds toward Caribbean sunrises or Nichupté Lagoon sunsets. A 2026 renovation refreshed this Cancún landmark without sacrificing its theatrical streak. Days might involve salsa lessons, pickleball, or children gleefully getting drenched beneath splash-park tipping buckets. Included meals feature freshly pressed tortillas at Taqueria Blue Agave and ceviche at Agua Marina, and bars pour Patrón and Grey Goose without a surcharge. For a quieter stay, The Reserve upgrade tier adds an adults-only pool, restaurant, and concierge service.

Here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Not all Cancún resorts are sprawling tropical compounds. At Secrets The Vine, a sleek adults-only tower brings a more cosmopolitan beach experience, with teak furnishings, Italian porcelain floors, and balconies suspended over that improbable Caribbean blue. As the name suggests, afternoons and evenings are devoted to the grape. Sommelier-led tastings gather guests around a handcrafted wooden table at the Vine Bar; evenings bring Mexican and international pours, and between glasses, a white-sand beach and three infinity pools tempt you outside. While many wines and premium spirits are included, special bottles from the cellar carry additional charges but are well worth it.

Dinner without one eye on a restless toddler is a luxury Finest Playa Mujeres has thought to provide. At Imagine Lounge, staff look after potty-trained children ages three and older for up to 90 minutes while parents eat nearby. The practical details are equally reassuring: homemade baby purées, bottle warmers, and family suites with a separate bedroom for the children. Meals, drinks, and 24-hour room service are included, so parents can order dinner after the little ones are asleep. One Spa even offers treatments for younger guests, though those appointments cost extra.

At Almare’s swim-up bar, the rum is blended with coconut or mango; at Botanik, the coffee is Mexican and locally roasted. Those touches give this 109-room, adults-only retreat on Isla Mujeres a sense of place. Get better acquainted through a tikin xic cooking experience devoted to the island’s signature fish dish, or take a kayak out from the beach—all complimentary. There’s a pool by the shore and an infinity pool on the rooftop, where dinner at Seasalt comes with Caribbean views and Mexican-European cooking. The resort also arranges guided visits to Punta Sur’s temple ruins for a fee, where you’ll hear stories of the Maya goddess Ixchel.

Excellence Playa Mujeres is a place to spread out—even the entry-level suites are upwards of 800 square feet, with whirlpool tubs and furnished terraces. Book a rooftop suite, and you can spend the afternoon between your plunge pool and daybed, with lunch delivered whenever you’re ready. Venture downstairs, though, and there's so much more: winding pools lead past swim-up terraces, beach waiters keep the margaritas coming, and dinner could mean Indian curries at Basmati or a lingering French meal at Chez Isabelle. Club suites at this adults-only Playa Mujeres retreat add private pools and beach areas and one Miilé Spa hydrotherapy session per person, per stay.

What is the best all-inclusive resort in Cancún?

For an adult-only stay, Le Blanc Spa Resort Cancún gets my vote. Butler service and French tasting menus make it feel suitably indulgent, and the rate includes access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit. With children, I’d choose Finest Playa Mujeres, where separate kids' bedrooms and supervised care during mealtimes give parents a holiday too.

Is it worth getting an all-inclusive package in Cancún?

Yes, especially if you plan to spend most of your vacation at the resort. At the right property, your rate covers dinners you actually look forward to, premium drinks, and activities you’d otherwise pay for separately. If you plan to spend each day exploring and eating around town, a traditional hotel may make more sense. Before booking your all-inclusive, be sure to check the exclusions—you might find you'll have to pay extra for spa treatments, special bottles of wine, and some restaurant experiences.

What’s the cheapest month to go to Cancún?

September is generally one of the cheapest months for Cancún hotels, after summer vacation crowds leave. The trade-off is wetter weather and the possibility of tropical storms during hurricane season. For a better balance of price and weather, consider late October through the week before Thanksgiving.

How we choose the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6234. United Unveils 14-Gate Concourse at Dulles

United and the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority unveiled Washington Dulles International Airport’s first new concourse in nearly two decades on Monday. Concourse E opens to passengers Nov. 10, giving United 14 new gates at a hub where its departures have risen 30% since 2022.

The 435,000-square-foot concourse connects directly to the airport’s AeroTrain and has jet bridges at every gate. It can handle both domestic and international flights. The airports authority said existing gates were already fully in use several times a day, with passengers crowding waiting areas and concessions during peak periods.

The concourse also houses United’s second-largest United Club. The nearly 40,000-square-foot lounge seats more than 600 people and increases the airline’s total lounge space at Dulles by about 70%. New concessions include local businesses such as Good Company Doughnuts & Café and Honor Brewing.

“Washington Dulles is a critical part of United’s global network and growth strategy,” United CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement. The carrier currently offers more than 250 daily flights from Dulles to 135 destinations.

United has added six international destinations from the airport this year. It plans to begin international Airbus A321XLR service from Dulles in December with flights to Amsterdam and Dublin, followed by new service to Toulouse, France, and Milan in 2027.

Concourse E is the first phase of the broader Dulles Global Gateway program, which United and the airports authority estimate will involve more than $20 billion in investment. Later work is expected to add gates, expand the main terminal, and build a new U.S. Customs facility. The program also calls for extending the AeroTrain so the airport can eventually retire its mobile lounges.
